hpi_details: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with hematuria, periorbital edema, and hypertension. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: thinks it might be connected to the sore throat she had a couple of weeks ago
concerns: She is worried the high blood pressure and swollen face mean she is on the verge of having a stroke before her daughter's upcoming wedding.
expectations: She hopes to be prescribed strong antibiotics to flush out any remaining infection and something to safely bring her blood pressure down today.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes supportive care with sodium and fluid restriction, loop diuretics for volume overload, and antihypertensives for blood pressure control, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: hematuria, periorbital edema, and hypertension

Key HPI features: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with hematuria, periorbital edema, and hypertension. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 162/98, HR 82, RR 16, afebrile. Periorbital and mild bilateral lower-extremity edema. Labs: Urinalysis with tea/cola-colored urine, dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, 1-2+ proteinuria. Serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (elevated from baseline), low C3 complement, elevated ASO titer and anti-DNase B confirming recent streptococcal infection.
Relevant background/PMH: Unremarkable; sore throat approximately 2 weeks prior, untreated
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to IgA nephropathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypertension or oliguria.
management_principles: Start supportive care: sodium and fluid restriction, plus a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) for volume overload and blood pressure control
Add an antihypertensive (e.g., amlodipine) if blood pressure remains elevated despite diuresis
Monitor renal function and urine output closely; refer to nephrology for renal biopsy if renal function worsens or features suggest rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: hematuria, periorbital edema, and hypertension

A 38-year-old female presents with cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and new hypertension beginning about 10 days after an untreated sore throat. Reports mild fatigue and headache; denies dysuria, rash, or joint pain.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 162/98, HR 82, RR 16, afebrile. Periorbital and mild bilateral lower-extremity edema. Labs: Urinalysis with tea/cola-colored urine, dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, 1-2+ proteinuria. Serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (elevated from baseline), low C3 complement, elevated ASO titer and anti-DNase B confirming recent streptococcal infection.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, presenting with nephritic syndrome (hematuria, edema, hypertension) approximately 10 days after streptococcal pharyngitis, supported by low C3 and positive ASO/anti-DNase B.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Sodium and fluid restriction with a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) for volume overload and blood pressure control. 2. Add an antihypertensive (e.g., amlodipine) if blood pressure remains elevated. 3. Monitor renal function, urine output, and blood pressure closely; most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks. 4. Refer to nephrology for renal biopsy if renal function worsens or features suggest rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Supportive care, blood pressure control, loop diuretics

teaching.one_liner: Immune complex deposition after a streptococcal throat infection causes acute nephritic syndrome with hematuria, periorbital edema, and hypertension.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 162/98 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and oriented, appearing mildly fatigued with visible puffiness around both eyes, but in no acute distress.
Prominent bilateral periorbital edema present; conjunctivae pink and sclerae non-icteric; extraocular movements intact.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal erythema, tonsillar exudate, or posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning.
Normal heart sounds with regular rhythm; no audible heart murmur, gallop, or pericardial friction rub.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without crackles, rales, or wheezing.
Abdomen is flat and soft with no tenderness, palpable masses, hepatosplenomegaly, or suprapubic distension.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle fist percussion bilaterally.
Mild 1+ pitting edema noted over the bilateral pretibial areas and medial malleoli.
Skin is warm and dry without petechiae, purpura, palpable rash, or evidence of active impetigo.
